title: Doubt is running on Broadway through 4/21 #broadway #theatre #doubt #...
transcript: This weekend I saw the first Broadway revival of doubt, starring Amy Ryan Lee of Schreiber, Zoe Kazan, and Quincy Tyler Bernstein. Play was written 20 years ago, and it got the Pulitzer and the Tony and an Oscar nominated film adaptation. Despite all of that, though, this was actually my first exposure to it. The play grew on me as it went along. At first I was a little thrown off by, like, surprisingly comedic in the beginning, and Scott Ellis's direction leans into it in a way that I was a little bit like, what play am I watching? The script definitely gets more serious as it goes, but I don't think the production ever quite course corrected. I felt like these actors were playing kind of cartoonish caricature versions of their roles, which was really weird. With the exception of the EV Schreiber, I did like his performance, but the rest of them, I don't know. I like all of these actors, but the way they were directed really missed the Mark for me. But luckily, as I got into the play more, I was able to kind of forget about it. So now, speaking of the play itself, at first I had a similar nagging feeling that I had at the hunt at Saint Anne's Warehouse, which was like, do we really need a play that effectively amplifies the message of casting doubt on abuse victims? But in retrospect, I don't think that's what John Patrick Shanley was doing at all. He's not encouraging the audience to doubt as much as he's asking, when you encounter doubt, which you inevitably will in some situations, because life is messy, how will you wrestle with it and reconcile with it on your path to trying to do the right thing? I obviously didn't see this play 20 years ago, but I have to imagine that this question resonates almost more strongly in 2024, in this age of information, where we're all a little bit terrified of doubt, you know, like, we all wanna know for sure, and when we don't, we sometimes have a tendency to convince ourselves that we do rather than just, like, accepting that there is doubt. But we have to move forward and do the best with the information we have. Anyway, I am curious to watch the movie now because I suspect that I'll like it more than I like this production. But I'm glad I got to see it live anyway, because there's something about being in an audience and collectively reacting to and processing this play, and it's difficult questions that I do think is important to the experience.
